problem-solving-process-story.text: AJ starts the final week by choosing one problem that still feels real in his chest, not just one that sounds impressive on a slide. He wants the presentation to begin with a lived frustration people can recognize right away.

Nia cuts out every exaggerated claim and rewrites the setup so the crew names the actual user, the actual pain point, and the actual limit of what their solution can do. If the explanation is honest, the audience can trust the rest.

Malik lays out the evidence trail: the questions they asked, the comments and examples they collected, and the pattern that kept showing up. The point is not to drown people in data. The point is to show that the build came from proof, not guessing.

AJ and Malik turn the messy building process into a clean story: first prompt, rough prototype, broken version, feedback, and stronger revision. Now the audience can see the workflow instead of imagining magic.

With the facts in place, the crew shapes the final talk into one clear arc: here is the problem, here is what we learned, here is what we built, and here is why it matters. Week 4 is not about sounding polished. It is about making the learning visible.

capstone-journey-story.text: AJ practices opening with the exact moment the problem became impossible to ignore. That hook matters because it reminds the audience that the capstone began in real life, not in a random assignment prompt.

Nia listens like a tough editor. Every time the crew says always, everyone, or best, she stops them and asks for proof. If they cannot defend a claim with evidence from the project, it does not make the final version.

Malik gets the live demo ready by checking the flow, saving screenshots, and preparing a backup path in case the internet acts strange. A strong presentation is not only about confidence. It is about planning for reality.

The crew runs the talk for a small practice audience and listens for the moment people lean in, get confused, or ask follow-up questions. That reaction becomes feedback they can actually use before the final presentation.

AJ tightens the hook, Nia cleans the logic, and Malik sharpens the demo sequence. The final version is stronger because they tested it in public first. That is the Week 4 move: test, sharpen, present.

portfolio-celebration-story.text: When the portfolio comes together, Malik makes sure it leads with evidence: the problem statement, the research trail, the build decisions, and the finished capstone. The portfolio is not decoration. It is proof that the crew can solve real problems.

AJ presents without apologizing for what is unfinished. He focuses on what the crew learned, what the tool does right now, and why the problem was worth solving. Confidence here means ownership, not pretending the work is perfect.

Nia handles tough questions by staying grounded. If the answer is known, she gives it plainly. If the answer is not known yet, she says what the crew would test next. Honest answers make the presentation stronger than fake certainty ever could.

Malik opens the repo, the prompts, and the working demo to show the actual workflow behind the final product. The audience gets to see that this crew does not just talk about ideas. They can document, build, and iterate in public.

By the end, AJ, Nia, and Malik are not framed as kids who completed a course. They are framed as problem solvers who can notice a need, investigate it, build a response, and explain their thinking. That is the real graduation moment.
